chunks: “His blood is not left unavenged, but rather the blood-money is to be paid.”
810-15 — Hammad, from Ibn al-Mughirah, from Ibn Sinan: the like of it.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because the diyah only becomes binding upon the people of the village and the tribe among whom the slain person is found when they are accused of his killing and they refuse the qasamah, according to what we have mentioned previously. But if they are not accused of his killing, or they respond to the qasamah, then there is no diyah upon them, and the diyah of the slain person is paid from the Bayt al-mal, according to what we have mentioned in the chapter of qasamah. That which further clarifies this is what he narrated:
14 — From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Ibn Sinan, from Abi Abdillah عليه السلام:

key_terms.الدِّيَةَ: financial compensation due for unlawful killing
key_terms.الْقَتِيلُ: the slain person whose killer is not identified
key_terms.الْقَسَامَةِ: the formal oath procedure used in homicide claims
key_terms.بَيْتِ الْمَالِ: the public treasury from which compensation may be paid
key_terms.دَمُهُ: the blood of the slain person, meaning his wrongful killing is not to be disregarded
key_terms.مُتَّهَمِينَ: those suspected or accused of the killing
key_terms.يُعْقَلُ: the diyah is to be borne and paid

ai.seo_question: When is the diyah for an unidentified slain person paid by the local people, and when is it paid from the Bayt al-mal?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the legal ruling concerning an unidentified killing and the payment of diyah. It explains that liability falls upon the people among whom the victim was found only when they are under accusation and refuse the qasamah; otherwise, the diyah is paid from the Bayt al-mal.
